# A global support stress at a fixed-cap volume maximizer

This is a first-order consequence of the actual maximum-volume problem in
`candidate b989614dc4f86228`. It does not claim that arbitrary
attained depth minimizers are polytopal. The lemma applies when the given
maximizing family has full-dimensional polytopal fibers. The separate proof
in `candidate 21db6cba533d25dc` obtains such an attained object
from any strict fixed-P counterexample, unless zero-volume fibers first
give a strict support reduction.

## 1. Precise hypotheses

Fix finite P and finitely many fixed nonvertical caps

    H_j={(z,x):v_j.z+u_j.x>=b_j},      |u_j|=1.

Suppose an actual compatible family K=(K_z) of full-dimensional polytopes
maximizes total mixed volume M among compatible families over P subject to
fixed cap budgets mu(H_j)<=B_j. Let J be the active cap constraints. Assume
B_j=mu(H_j)>0 for j in J. In the depth-minimizer application the common
budget is beta M, so every j in J has mass beta M.

There are nonnegative numbers lambda_j, not all zero, and a nonnegative
stress on the active homogeneous inequalities of a finite compatible-support
cone, satisfying the equation proved below. The same lambda_j apply
simultaneously to every fiber. Facet coincidences with cap boundaries are
retained through explicit coefficients in [0,1]; no transversality
assumption is used.

## 2. A finite support cone containing common erosion

Choose a common complete fan on which the support functions of all K_z and
of their sufficiently small common inner parallel bodies K_z minus t B_d
are linear. Such a finite fan exists for polytopes. Indeed the inner parallel
body is defined by shifting each original unit-normal facet offset by -t.
Every candidate vertex is affine in t, and its feasibility is given by
finitely many affine inequalities in t. Hence the combinatorial type and
normal fan are constant for 0<t<t_0. Take a common refinement over the
finitely many fibers and the original fans, then a simplicial refinement.
The support values of the erosion family on this fan are affine in t.
When preserving a facet bound, additionally require each fiber support
function to remain linear on its OWN small-erosion fan. These are linear
conditions in the common-refinement coordinates and introduce no new facet
normals in that fiber. All directions used below, including erosion,
dilation, and affine fiber translations, remain available.

Use support values on its rays as coordinates h, restricted to the linear
subspace expressing linearity on nonsimplicial cones if needed. Support
convexity and all actual fiber-compatibility conditions form finitely many
homogeneous linear inequalities A h>=0, as proved in
`candidate 94a1565e143d393e`. At the given array h_* let
A_0 consist of the active rows, and put

    D={delta : A_0 delta>=0}.

Every delta in D gives a compatible support array h_*+t delta for all
sufficiently small t>=0. Full-dimensionality persists for these small
perturbations.

Common erosion preserves compatibility exactly. From
sum_w p_w K_w subset K_z, with sum p_w=1, one gets

    sum_w p_w(K_w minus tB_d)+tB_d
       =sum_w p_w[(K_w minus tB_d)+tB_d]
       subset sum_w p_w K_w subset K_z.

Thus sum_w p_w(K_w minus tB_d) subset K_z minus tB_d. All fibers remain
nonempty for t below their minimum inradius. Its support derivative e belongs
to D and has value -1 at every original unit-normal facet.

## 3. All cap derivative possibilities form an explicit finite set

For a facet F of K_z let n_F be its outward unit normal and |F| its
(d-1)-volume. In dimension one use counting measure on endpoint facets.
The volume derivative is the linear functional

    L_0(delta)=sum_(z,F) |F| delta_z(n_F).

If the cap boundary does not contain F, its contribution to the cap
derivative is

    |F intersect int(H_j)_z| delta_z(n_F).

If the cap boundary contains F, the contribution is one of

    0,                     |F| delta_z(n_F),

according to the sign of its velocity and the side containing K_z. More
explicitly, it is |F|min(delta_z(n_F),0) if K_z lies inside the cap, and
|F|max(delta_z(n_F),0) if K_z lies outside the cap.

These statements follow by the swept-prism formula. Facets move with normal
speed delta_z(n_F); neighborhoods of edges and of transverse intersections
with the fixed cap plane contribute o(t). A coincident facet contributes
only its inward or outward swept prism on the cap's side, giving the stated
minimum or maximum. Newly appearing zero-area facets contribute o(t).

Let G_j be the finite set of linear functionals obtained by independently
choosing coefficient 0 or |F| at every coincident facet and using the fixed
coefficients elsewhere. The actual one-sided cap derivative in any delta
belongs to these choices, and in particular is at most

    max_(L in G_j) L(delta).

Moreover EVERY L in G_j satisfies L(e)<0 for j in J. The boundary portion
of at least one positive-volume cap section inside the OPEN cap has positive
(d-1)-area, since that cap has positive mass. It contributes its negative
area under erosion, and every remaining term is nonpositive. Thus there is
a genuine common strict-decrease direction for all active cap gradients.

## 4. Finite-dimensional separation gives the global stress

There cannot be delta in D such that

    L(delta)<=0 for every L in every G_j, j in J,
    L_0(delta)>0.

Otherwise add a sufficiently small positive multiple of e. The objective
derivative remains positive and ALL the finitely many active cap-gradient
possibilities become strictly negative. For sufficiently small t the
compatible family h_*+t(delta+epsilon e) would satisfy every active budget
strictly, retain all inactive budget inequalities by continuity, and increase
volume. This contradicts actual maximality.

The finite-dimensional Farkas alternative therefore gives

    L_0 = sum_(j in J) lambda_j L_j - eta^T A_0,

where lambda_j>=0, eta>=0, and L_j belongs to conv(G_j). In facet form write

    L_j(delta)=sum_(z,F) a_(j,z,F) delta_z(n_F),

where a_(j,z,F)=|F intersect int(H_j)_z| at noncoincident facets, and

    a_(j,z,F)=theta_(j,z,F)|F|,       0<=theta_(j,z,F)<=1,

at coincident facets. These boundary coefficients are part of the certificate,
not discarded boundary mass. Some lambda_j must be positive: evaluating the
stress at the dilation direction h_* gives L_0(h_*)=dM>0, while
A_0 h_*=0 by homogeneity, so lambda_j=0 for all j is impossible.

This is a normalized objective multiplier, rather than a possibly abnormal
Fritz-John certificate. The common erosion direction is what justifies the
finite separation argument with the objective coefficient fixed at one.

## 5. Explicit simultaneous translation and shear balances

For each cap and fiber put t_j(z)=b_j-v_j.z. Define an effective section area
s_(j,z) as follows:

* If the plane u_j.x=t_j(z) meets int(K_z), use its ordinary (d-1)-section area.
* If the plane lies strictly outside K_z, or only meets a face of dimension
  below d-1, use zero.
* If it contains a facet F and K_z is inside H_j, use (1-theta_(j,z,F))|F|.
* If it contains a facet F and K_z is outside H_j, use theta_(j,z,F)|F|.

All these numbers are nonnegative. For a translation vector c of one fiber,
the cap functional satisfies

    L_j(c at fiber z)=s_(j,z) u_j.c.

This follows by the divergence theorem on a truncated polytope. At a
coincident facet the two displayed trace cases follow by adding or deleting
its normal-area contribution. Thus it also holds with boundary facets.

Every affine point array ell_z(u)=u.(Bz+b) is lineality of the compatible
support cone. Hence A_0 ell=0 and L_0(ell)=0. Evaluating the stress on all
such affine translations yields the GLOBAL equations

    sum_j lambda_j u_j sum_z s_(j,z) = 0,

    sum_j lambda_j u_j [sum_z s_(j,z) z]^T = 0.

The first is a vector balance in R^d; the second is a d by n matrix balance.
They coordinate cap-section areas across all fibers, with one common set of
nonnegative cap weights. They are stronger than independent per-fiber
facet stationarity.

Finally the same truncated-polytope divergence identity gives

    L_j(h_*)=d mu(H_j)+sum_z t_j(z) s_(j,z).

Evaluating the stress at h_* removes the homogeneous compatibility stress:

    dM = d sum_j lambda_j mu(H_j)
                 + sum_(j,z) lambda_j t_j(z) s_(j,z).

For the exact critical-cap problem all active masses equal beta M, so

    1 = beta sum_j lambda_j
                 + [sum_(j,z)lambda_j t_j(z)s_(j,z)]/(dM).

This tracks the exact value beta and all boundary terms. No estimate of the
last signed offset term, and no simplex or hollow-support classification,
has been proved here. Those would require a genuinely additional argument.
